nodes.description:
Western blotting of patient material shows not only a deficiency of the NDUFS8 polypeptide itself - which a mutation in its own gene would produce trivially - but reductions in other nuclear-encoded subunits of complex I as well. That second observation is the informative one: the rest of the complex cannot be maintained without TYKY, so the subunit is required for assembly, for stability of the assembled enzyme, or for both. The available data do not distinguish those alternatives, and the reporting authors do not claim to.
There is a structural proposal for what the subunit is doing. NDUFS8/TYKY is thought to connect the membrane and peripheral domains of complex I - the boundary between the arm embedded in the inner membrane and the arm that carries the electron relay. A subunit at that junction is exactly the kind whose loss would destabilise the whole assembly rather than remove one catalytic step. Consistent with that, the late-onset patient also showed a drastic reduction in the 39-kDa subunit, which is proposed to sit at the same domain boundary and may interact with TYKY directly.
nodes.id: Complex I Assembly and Stability Failure

nodes.description: Primary skin fibroblasts from Leigh syndrome patients with isolated complex I deficiency, including NDUFS8-mutant lines, cultured in pyruvate-free medium with galactose replacing glucose. The medium is the model: it forbids glycolytic compensation, so the bioenergetic deficit that patient cells normally paper over becomes lethal to them and not to controls. It is a conditional model - in ordinary glucose medium the same cells survive.

A compensatory response that is also a methodological trap, and the reason it is curated as a node rather than left as a footnote. Cells with complex I deficiency upregulate glycolysis to replace lost mitochondrial ATP, and that adaptation masks other consequences of the deficiency. Replacing glucose with galactose in a pyruvate-free medium removes the glycolytic escape route: under those conditions patient fibroblasts die while control cells do not.
Clinically the same logic explains why these patients decompensate under catabolic stress, and why a resting biochemical measurement can understate how close to the edge a tissue is.
Glycolysis is not the only compensatory response in play. In the late-onset patient's skeletal muscle the mitochondrially encoded complex IV COI subunit was ELEVATED while complex I protein was reduced, which the reporting authors read as an attempt to compensate by inducing mitochondrial gene expression. That is hedged as a reading rather than a demonstration, but it is worth recording: an assay that finds one respiratory complex up and another down should not be assumed to have gone wrong.
nodes.id: Glycolytic Compensation Masking the Bioenergetic Deficit

nodes.description:
Fibroblasts from children with nuclear complex I gene defects, including NDUFS8, show raised reactive oxygen species. The interesting finding is not the ROS itself but what happens when it is removed: chronic treatment with the water-soluble vitamin E derivative Trolox dramatically lowers ROS and is accompanied by a substantial increase in the amount of complex I. The reporting authors read that as evidence that complex I expression is itself regulated by ROS, which makes this node a feedback modifier on the assembly node rather than a terminal consequence.
It is curated PROVISIONAL because the causal claim rests on the correlated response to one intervention in cultured fibroblasts, and because the authors describe the contribution of ROS to pathogenesis as supported by circumstantial evidence.

nodes.description: The clinical endpoint, and the striking thing about it in this entity is its range rather than its severity. The index patient had neuropathologically proven Leigh syndrome with a progressive course ending in death in the first months of life - the presentation a core-subunit defect predicts. But a second patient had late-onset disease with only a partial complex I defect, and three siblings from a consanguineous family presented as "progressive external ophthalmoplegia plus", a picture in which nobody would have thought to sequence this gene. The authors of that report make the methodological point explicitly: untargeted exome analysis can re-write a phenotype.

nodes.description:
NDUFS8 encodes TYKY, a structural core subunit of complex I rather than an accessory one. Two features make it a plausible point of failure. It is highly conserved across eukaryotes and prokaryotes, which is the signature of a subunit whose sequence is constrained by an essential function rather than tolerated as scaffolding. And it carries two 4Fe4S ferredoxin consensus patterns that have long been thought to provide the binding site for iron-sulfur cluster N-2 - the terminal cluster of the electron relay, the one that delivers electrons to ubiquinone.
Reported pathogenic alleles are missense: C236T (p.Pro79Leu) and G305A (p.Arg102His) as compound heterozygotes in the index patient, two further novel missense changes in the late-onset patient, and homozygous variants in the consanguineous "PEO plus" family.

evidence.snippet: The nuclear-encoded NDUFS8 (TYKY) subunit of complex I is highly conserved among eukaryotes and prokaryotes and contains two 4Fe4S ferredoxin consensus patterns, which have long been thought to provide the binding site for the iron-sulfur cluster N-2.

evidence.snippet: The first mutation was a C236T (P79L), and the second mutation was a G305A (R102H).

evidence.snippet: NDUFS8 is a nuclear-encoded structural core protein of complex I, and mutations are expected to cause infantile onset and severe disease.

nodes.description:
Human umbilical vein and other endothelial cells with NDUFS8 silenced by shRNA or deleted by CRISPR/Cas9. This is the only NDUFS8-specific loss-of-function model in the cited literature, and its value here is that it isolates NDUFS8 from the other complex I genes that the patient-fibroblast panels unavoidably pool. It reproduces the bioenergetic lesion cleanly: reduced oxygen consumption and complex I activity, decreased ATP, mitochondrial depolarization, raised ROS and lipid oxidation.
What it also reports - an NDUFS8-dependent ATP-Akt-mTOR-angiogenesis axis, with retinal angiogenesis inhibited in vivo by endothelial-specific knockdown - is deliberately NOT curated as a disease mechanism on this entry. Endothelial cells are not the tissue that fails in MC1DN2, vascular maldevelopment is not a reported patient phenotype, and the paper's own framing is about angiogenesis biology rather than about this disease. The open question is recorded as a HUMAN_MODEL_MISMATCH discussion instead.

nodes.description: A bypass rather than a disease model. Yeast Ndi1p is a single-subunit alternative NADH dehydrogenase that oxidizes NADH and reduces ubiquinone without pumping protons, so expressing it in a complex I-deficient nematode restores the electron path around the missing enzyme. It complements a complex I-deficient C. elegans strain with improvements in reproduction and whole-organism respiration, which is what makes it a tool for asking which complex I defects are bypassable - and, by extension, a proof of principle for gene-therapy-style bypass in NDUFS8-type core-subunit disease.
nodes.id: Ndi1p-expressing Caenorhabditis elegans complex I bypass model

nodes.description:
The step at which this entity's biochemistry says something the assembly story alone does not. In control fibroblasts the ratio between complex I enzymatic activity and complex I amount is exactly one - enzyme present is enzyme working. In fibroblasts from children with nuclear complex I gene defects including NDUFS8 that ratio falls below one. The enzyme that does get assembled is therefore intrinsically impaired, not merely scarce.
That is what a core subunit carrying the terminal iron-sulfur cluster would be expected to do, and it distinguishes this entity mechanistically from the accessory-subunit deficiencies elsewhere in the nuclear complex I series, where the lesion is essentially one of quantity. Practically, it also predicts a ceiling on any therapy that works by increasing the amount of complex I - see the antioxidant node.
nodes.id: Reduced Complex I Amount and Intrinsic Catalytic Activity

nodes.description: Fibroblasts from six children with isolated complex I deficiency caused by mutations in NDUFS1, NDUFS2, NDUFS7, NDUFS8 or NDUFV1, treated chronically with the water-soluble vitamin E derivative Trolox. Used here as a perturbation of the ROS node rather than as a disease model: it asks what happens to complex I when oxidative stress is removed.

An obligate aerobic yeast whose complex I is the standard genetic system for this enzyme, used here to test the actual patient alleles rather than a knockout. This is the most disease-specific model available for this entity: unlike the fibroblast panels, which pool NDUFS8 with four other genes, and unlike the C. elegans bypass, which addresses complex I deficiency in general, it asks directly whether P85L and R138H are pathogenic. The reporting authors introduced them into the Y. lipolytica homologue and treated the result as confirmation of biochemical significance.
